# From continuous systems to discrete models {#sec-discrete-continuous}

A finite element model is a discrete mathematical representation of a continuous
system.

In a discrete system, the state is described by a finite set of variables. In a
continuous system, the state is described by one or more fields defined over the
entire domain.

## A continuous system: a one-dimensional bar

![One-dimensional bar fixed at the left end, with distributed axial load $q$,
end force $F$, coordinate $x$, cross-sectional area $A$, Young's modulus $E$,
and axial displacement field
$u(x)$.](images/bar_in_tension-1d.png){
  #fig-bar-1d
  width=30%
}

A one-dimensional bar is a continuous body. Its axial displacement can be
evaluated at every point of the bar and is therefore represented by a function,

$$
  u=u(x).
$$

The displacement field is the primary variable of the problem. For a linearly
elastic bar,

$$
  \varepsilon(x)=\frac{du}{dx}=u'(x)
$$

is the axial strain and

$$
  \sigma(x)=E\varepsilon(x)
$$

is the axial stress. The corresponding internal axial force is

$$
  N(x)=\int_A \sigma\,dA.
$$

For a homogeneous bar with constant $E$ and $A$,

$$
  N=EA\frac{du}{dx}.
$$

Equilibrium under the distributed axial load $q$ gives

$$
  \frac{dN}{dx}+q=0,
$$

and hence

$$
  EA\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}=-q.
$$

![Cross-section $A$ with axial stress $\sigma_x$, represented equivalently by
the internal axial force $N$. A positive internal force corresponds to
tension.](images/bar-cross-section.png){
  #fig-bar-cross-section
  width=30%
}

The state of the bar is therefore described by the complete displacement field
$u(x)$, which contains information at an infinite number of points.

## A discrete system: a one-dimensional spring

A spring is already a discrete mechanical system. Its state can be described by
quantities defined only at its end points.

![One-dimensional spring of stiffness $k_s$ between end points 1 and 2. The end
displacements $u_1$ and $u_2$ and the nodal forces are referred to the positive
$x$ direction.](images/spring-1d.png){
  #fig-spring-1d
  width=30%
}

The spring elongation or spring stretch is a measure of the spring deformation
and is defined as

$$
  \delta=u_2-u_1.
$$

A positive elongation corresponds to a stretched spring. The internal spring
force is related to the elongation by

$$
  F_s=k_s\delta,
$$

where $k_s$ is the spring stiffness.

![Positive sign convention for the internal spring force $F_s$: outward forces
at the two sides of a cut spring indicate
tension.](images/spring-1d-convention.png){
  #fig-spring-1d-convention
  width=30%
}

The relation

$$
  F_s=k_s\delta
$$

plays the same role for the spring that the constitutive relation
$\sigma=E\varepsilon$ plays for the bar. The deformation measure is now the
single scalar $\delta$, rather than the strain field $\varepsilon(x)$.

## Continuous and discrete descriptions

The state of the spring is determined by the two discrete quantities $u_1$ and
$u_2$. The state of the bar is described by the function $u(x)$.

The continuous description is richer: it provides the displacement at every
point, whereas the discrete description contains only a finite number of values.
A finite element model replaces the continuous field by a finite set of unknowns
while retaining enough information to approximate the mechanical response.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why begin with springs?

A spring is already discrete, so no approximation of a continuous field is
needed. It can therefore be used to introduce equilibrium, element matrices,
assembly, boundary conditions, and the global system of equations before those
same ideas are applied to continuous bodies.
:::

The next chapter uses two springs in series to derive the direct stiffness
method and the algebraic system

$$
  \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}.
$$
